strengths: Well-motivated and systematic formalization of evaluation protocols (R1, H1, H2, H3, T1, T2) addressing real comparability issues across different ASR systems and model types
Comprehensive experimental design with stratified analysis across multiple dimensions: transcript quality, audio encoders, duration, speaker composition, and detailed hand-crafted feature ablations

Strong empirical insights from research questions, particularly: ASR quality doesn't directly predict segmentation performance, pause duration accounts for ~95% of acoustic feature gains, and clear identification of duration/speaker composition effects on model performance
AudioSeg substantially outperforms text-based approaches on shorter audio (<30 min) by directly leveraging learned audio representations without requiring transcription
High reproducibility with detailed appendices covering hyperparameters, feature extraction methodology, prompts, augmented dataset annotations, and commitment to release code
weaknesses: Single-dataset evaluation (YTSeg, English only, YouTube-specific) severely limits generalizability. Authors acknowledge YTSeg is currently the only large-scale dataset, but this undermines confidence in methodological recommendations and findings applicability

Limited technical novelty: AudioSeg architecture is straightforward (frozen encoder → local transformers → document encoder); performance is heavily encoder-dependent (Whisper Large F1=45.52 vs. Qwen3-AuT F1=24.66), suggesting gains derive primarily from encoder choice rather than architecture

Modest practical improvements without statistical significance testing: AudioSeg shows ~5-8 F1 point gains over text-based models overall, but performance converges for longer content (F1=13.28 vs. 15.17 at ≥60 min); hand-crafted features yield only +3.0 F1 total

AudioSeg performance degradation on longer audio (>20-30 min) is observed but inadequately explained and unresolved. Hypothesis about training data distribution lacks supporting evidence; potential architectural solutions unexplored

MLLM evaluation is limited and underwhelming: restricted to <30 minute videos due to context constraints, weak baseline performance (Qwen2.5-Omni: F1=3.43), and LoRA fine-tuning produces severe hallucinations (1032.6% transcript length). Claims about MLLM promise are overstated

Proposed time-based evaluation protocols (T1, T2) lack complete empirical validation: Table A6 shows T1 maintains ranking consistency with existing text-space protocols (somewhat undermining necessity argument); T2 (continuous-time) is never experimentally evaluated despite being the most novel contribution
No cross-validation, multiple runs with different seeds, or statistical significance tests despite some improvements being modest, limiting confidence in reported gains

Non-speech audio cues (music, sound effects) validated only through single ablation (Table A1: -2.21 F1 with DeepFilterNet). Insufficient analysis of when and how much this contributes to AudioSeg's advantage

strengths: Clear problem motivation addressing real gaps in existing transcript-centric audio chaptering research
Formalized evaluation protocols (T1, T2) that enable fair transcript-invariant comparison across modeling paradigms—a solid methodological contribution
Comprehensive experimental design systematically addressing five clear research questions with stratified analysis by duration, speaker regime, and domain
Significant reproducibility contribution: large-scale dataset (19.3K videos) with duration/speaker annotations, detailed hyperparameters, feature extraction methodology, and promised toolkit release

Actionable empirical findings: pause duration dominates acoustic gains (+2.87 F1); speaker features provide targeted improvements (+2.95 F1 in multi-speaker); joint training on reference+ASR improves robustness
Well-organized writing with clear motivation, methods, and presentation of results
weaknesses: Severe dataset limitation: primary reliance on YTSeg (YouTube, English-only); AMI validation uses only 25 evaluation videos; poor cross-domain transfer (Qwen3 F1: 41.30→9.16) suggests findings are YouTube-specific and lack generalizability

AudioSeg's source of improvement unclear: performance varies dramatically by encoder (Whisper Large 45.52 vs HuBERT 35.58 vs PEA-Frame 31.36), suggesting encoder choice (with domain match to YouTube) drives results, not architectural novelty; architecture itself is standard

Evaluation protocol may favor AudioSeg: T1 uses 6-second chunks matching AudioSeg's native resolution while text models are mapped to this grid; Table A8 shows non-monotonic behavior at non-aligned chunk sizes; oracle analysis (Table A7) shows 20% F1 discretization loss yet is treated as technical detail

MLLM evaluation incomplete: limited to <30 min videos, only Qwen models, task conflates transcription+segmentation+titling, unable to fine-tune Qwen3-Omni due to computational constraints, temporal grounding bottleneck (11.8s median error) unclear whether fundamental or temporary

Acoustic feature analysis underdeveloped: pauses dominate (+2.87 F1) but other features contribute minimally; no statistical significance testing or investigation of why pitch/speaking rate/loudness fail; suggests hand-crafted feature approach may be wrong direction

ASR quality analysis incomplete: weak WER-segmentation correspondence unexplained; counterintuitive finding (ASRL-trained model underperforms ASRT) without investigation; missing analysis of which ASR error types matter for chaptering
Limited technical novelty: text-based contribution is simple concatenation+linear projection of features; AudioSeg architecture is standard; no architectural ablations isolating design choices
No statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, p-values, or multi-run variance analysis despite large dataset; single train/val/test split reported
Title generation under-evaluated: metrics relegated to appendix, two proposed evaluation protocols (TM, GC) lack strong justification, limited discussion of quality-importance tradeoff

Missing ablations and comparisons: no isolation of chunk-size effects on AudioSeg vs text models, limited breadth of text baselines beyond MiniSeg, no comparison with recent audio-based segmentation methods
